final_message:
All five versions build with their own build scripts and print the correct output for every test: the three provided samples (`s1`–`s3`) and seven of my own. Those seven were checked against a separate Python Dijkstra I wrote. Two of them are benchmark-size (300,000 nodes, 900,000 roads, 6 sources): one random graph and one long path, which gives very large distances. The others cover multiple roads between the same nodes, self-loops, unreachable nodes, N=1, and more roads than nodes.

## Algorithm
- **Graph:** the input file is read in one go and parsed by hand. The roads are stored in a compact adjacency layout (CSR, compressed sparse row): each node's neighbours sit together as (target, weight) pairs. Self-loops are dropped because they never shorten a path.
- **Search:** Dijkstra from each source using a **radix heap**. It works because the smallest distance taken from the queue never decreases. Stale queue entries are skipped. In C++ this cut the shortest-path time from about 600 ms with a binary heap to about 280 ms.
- **Output:** nodes come out of the queue in order of distance. R, TOTAL, FAR and NODE (smallest node at distance FAR) are collected as they come out, so no extra pass is needed.

## Main speed choices
- **C++:** the queue is keyed on distance only. My first try also packed the node id into the key, which added about 19 extra levels per entry and was much slower. Distances are 32-bit when the total length of all roads is below 2³², since no shortest path can be longer than that; otherwise 64-bit, chosen through a template. Output is written in binary mode so Windows doesn't turn `\n` into `\r\n`.
- **Java, C#, Go:** queue entries are just node ids, read against the current `dist[]`, with a "settled" flag. Distances are `long`/`int64`, queues are growable `int` arrays, and the bit-scan is the language's built-in (`Long.numberOfLeadingZeros`, `BitOperations.LeadingZeroCount`, `bits.Len64`).
  - Java puts the hot loop in its own method so the JIT optimises it fully.
  - C# uses `unsafe` pointers in the inner loop, and I set `<TieredCompilation>false</TieredCompilation>` in `solution.csproj` so it compiles straight to optimised code.
  - Go appends to reused slices and builds its output with `strconv.Append*`.
- **JavaScript:** typed arrays throughout. Distances use `Int32Array` when the total road length fits in 32 bits, so V8 stays on small-integer arithmetic; otherwise `Float64Array`, with a two-part bucket calculation for keys above 2³². I forced and tested the `Float64Array` path separately. TOTAL moves into a BigInt before it could pass 2⁵³, so it stays exact.

## Timings
On the 300,000-node random graph, 3 runs each, including process start:

| Version | Time |
|---|---|
| C++ | 430–530 ms |
| Go | 580–780 ms |
| C# | 900–1,100 ms |
| JavaScript | 1,130–1,210 ms |
| Java | 1,280–1,430 ms |

The machine was heavily loaded by other programs during these runs: a trivial loop in Node ran several times slower than usual, and C++ alone varied by almost 2×. Treat the numbers as a rough order only.

I left my small test files and scripts in `tools/` (`gen.py`, `ref.py`, `test.sh`, `bench.sh` and five small cases) and deleted the large generated inputs. The only process I stopped was a stray Python process my own command had started, by its process ID.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
